title.en: Kemush Creates the World and the Dry Bones of the Dead
title.zh: 克穆什造世與枯骨成人

region.en: Klamath Lake country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯湖故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'How Kemush Created the World' (Klamath)

summary.en: Kemush, Old Man of the Ancients, springs from the ashes of the northern lights at Morning Star's call and makes the flat earth, planting roots, pines, waterfowl and game. Then he and his daughter Evening Sky dance five nights with the spirits of the dark, gather their abandoned dry bones, and scatter them two by two across the land, where they become the first peoples, the chipmunk people and the Klamath.
summary.zh: 克穆什（古人老者）應晨星之呼自北極光灰燼中躍出，造平坦大地，植百草松杉、放水鳥野獸。後與女兒暮空於冥界舞火五夜，收攏鬼魂遺下的枯骨，兩兩撒於山川之間，骨化為原初諸族、花栗鼠人與克拉斯人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klamath folk-narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Collector's preface notes ceremonial and coarse content was excluded; no restricted ceremonial knowledge is reproduced. Category 'myth': sacred cosmogony preserved as folktale. Pin is symbolic, at Klamath Falls.

passages.text: In the time that was, Kemush, Old Man of the Ancients, slept in Yamsi, the Lodge of the North Wind. He had sprung quickly from the ashes of the northern lights and made the world at the call of Morning Star. At first Kaila, the earth, was flat and bare; then Kemush planted grass and camas roots in the valleys, set the pines and juniper on the steeps, and put the mallard and white goose on river and lake, the deer and foxes in the forest, the mountain sheep and grizzly among the rocks. All the earth was new except Shapashkeni, the rock, where was built the lodge of Sun and Moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 25 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sun halo Wanaka called Kemush from the lodge door, and together they followed the trail of Shel, the sun, to the edge of the dark; but the Indian, Maidu, was not yet created. Kemush and his daughter Evening Sky went down to the Place of the Dark, to the lodges of the spirits, and for five nights in a great circle about a vast fire they danced with the ghosts. The spirits were without number, like leaves on the trees; but when the sun called to the world, they became dry bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 25-26 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the fifth day, when the sun was new, Kemush rose and put the dry bones into a sack, and as he followed the sun's trail to the edge of the world he threw the bones away two by two — to the place of steepness, to the crawfish trail, to the snow-ridge, to the mountain of the great blue heron. The bones became Maidu the Indian, Aikspala the chipmunk people, and last of all Maklaks, the Klamath Indian. Then Kemush climbed to the top of the sun's trail, built his lodge there, and lives there still with Evening Sky and Wanaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 26 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Robe of Kemush

region.en: Klamath Lake country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯湖故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'The Robe of Kemush' (Klamath)

summary.en: Walking on his own new-made earth with only a rabbit blanket for a robe, the creator Kemush tries to shoot five lynxes sitting in a tree to make himself a mantle — and misses every one until all have fled, each miss shrinking his claims about what the robe will cover. He then kills an antelope, but the dead animal runs off wearing his pinned-together blanket, mocking the creator of the world.
summary.zh: 造世者克穆什僅披兔皮在初造的大地上行走，欲射樹上五隻山貓製裘，卻連連失手，山貓逐一竄逃，而他的自誇也隨之縮水。後雖殺得一隻羚羊，獸屍卻披著他以木刺別起的舊兔皮狂奔而去，令創世者受窘。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klamath folk-narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Comic tale about the creator; no ceremonial content. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Kemush, walking upon the earth after having created it, saw five lynxes sitting in a tree. He had on only a rabbit blanket, and tore it to pieces, saying the lynxes would be a good robe when he killed them. Stone after stone missed; one lynx after another jumped down and ran away, and each time Kemush counted what he had lost — a full mantle, then one that would only cover his back — until at last he stood crying his mourning-song while the last lynxes skipped away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 28 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Gathering the pieces, he pinned the blanket together with splinters and went on. Not far away an antelope with an aching tooth lay on a clearing; Kemush spread the blanket over it and kicked it dead, then hunted a stone knife to skin it. But a second antelope ran off behind him, and the dead one Kemush had killed rose and ran before him wearing the rabbit blanket on its back. Kemush cried out for it to stop, saying the people would make fun of it, wrapped in his old rag.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 28-29 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Qawaneca Creates the World and Calls the Sun

region.en: Klamath country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'How Qawaneca Created the World'

summary.en: In the beginning dark and windless, Qawaneca sits on a scrap of land in the middle of the water. Land comes to him trembling; he steadies it, floods away its sickness five times, and throws three rocks and two clods into the water to set the tides. Unable to make daylight alone, he calls a council of birds, learns the magic call of the sun from two wild geese, and sets the sun on its summer and winter tracks. From his hairs come snakes — one long serpent coiling five times around the world — and dogs, while the undying Mother of the South sends all the dead back as infants.
summary.zh: 太初無光無風，瓜瓦內卡坐於水中孤陸。新地顫巍而來，他按之使穩，五次以水洗去其病，投三石二土定潮汐。既不能自造白晝，遂召鳥類議事，從兩隻野雁習得喚日秘咒，命太陽循夏冬軌道而行。自髮中化出群蛇——一條巨蛇繞世五匝使其不散——復化出狗；南方不死之母收殮亡者，遣之轉世為嬰。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published creation narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. No ceremonial content. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: At first it was dark; there was neither wind nor rain, no people or animals. In the middle of the water, on a piece of land, sat Qawaneca by his fire, breathing the smoke of burning cedar, while on the land's edge stood another god who saw an ash tree to the north and a red cedar to the south — trees sacred above all others ever since. Something red appeared to the southwest: land coming. It touched their island but trembled, and Qawaneca pressed his hands over it to steady it. Where many die, he said, he would make much water and little land; where few die, much land and little water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 30 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Qawaneca chose three rocks and two pieces of earth and threw them one by one into the water; after the fifth throw mighty waves arose, dashing against the land and receding — thus the tides were formed. New land came muddy, and footprints appeared in it: 'That is sickness,' said Qawaneca, and four times he made the water cover the land; the fifth time he let the footprints alone, for five is a sacred number.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 30-31 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Still dark, Qawaneca called all the birds to a great council to learn how to make sunlight. One bird knew: far in the north was the sun, and two wild geese who had been there would teach the magic call if Qawaneca gave special privileges to all birds. He learned the secret, called the sun, and made its track — northward in summer, southward in winter. From two hairs pulled from his head came snakes, which made storms by blowing with their mouths; one long serpent coiled itself five times around the world so it would not fall apart. Two more hairs became dogs. Then a woman came from the south — the Mother who never dies, to whom all Indians return at death, and who sends them back as infants. Qawaneca now lives in the sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 31-32 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Duration of Life: Mole, Flybug and Garter Snake Argue
title.zh: 壽數之辯：鼴鼠、蟊蟲與草蛇

region.en: Klamath Lake country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯湖故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Duration of Life' (Klamath)

summary.en: After Kemush makes the Klamath people from a service-berry bush — laid in the sun, hence dark; the white people he lays in the shade beyond the sea — the first creatures argue over how long humans should live. Mole wants humans to dwindle into decrepitude, because the cruel will trample him; Garter Snake wants humans to shed their skins and grow young again as it does; Flybug votes with Mole. The snake's plea loses: humans age and shiver with old age, and never grow young again.
summary.zh: 克穆什以 service-berry 灌木造克拉斯人，置於日下故色深；白人則置於海外蔭處。其後鼴鼠、草蛇與蟊蟲爭論人之壽數：草蛇欲人如己蛻皮返老還童，鼴鼠與蟊蟲懼人踐踏，欲人衰朽。結果人之必老遂定，不得回春。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klamath narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. This is the Klamath 'deathless life lost in debate' episode — a messenger-fails/origin-of-death cluster story. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Kemush, Old Man of the Ancients, made the Klamath Lake people, Maklaks, from a service-berry bush, and the Kakalish people from skunks, creating them as he went northward. The Klamath Lake people he laid down in the sun's heat; the white people he laid in the shade — therefore the Maklaks are dark. The light-colored race he set beyond the sea, where he made a world for them. He made the mole, the flybug, and the garter snake as well, and when he had made them, they began to argue about man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 38 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mole said: 'I want human beings to live to great age — to be decrepit by age, and thus to shiver.' Garter Snake disagreed: shedding its skin as it spoke, it said, 'This way I want man to become: after having grown to great age, always to grow young again.' Flybug voted with Mole, saying, 'Many human beings, acting cruelly, will step on me and crush me.' Thus they argued, and the snake's promise of renewed youth was not granted: human beings age and shiver, and do not grow young again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 38-39 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: How Coyote Stole Fire from the Skookums

region.en: Southern Oregon (Klamath River country; symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 俄勒岡南部（克拉馬斯河故地；象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'How Coyote Stole Fire'

summary.en: The only fire in the world burns on a mountain top watched by three Skookums, who fear that men who steal it will grow as strong as they. Coyote sculks among the bushes until the dawn wind sends one Skookum shivering indoors, snatches a brand and races downhill. A relay of animals carries the fire — Wolf, Squirrel with its scorched black neck and curled tail, Frog losing its tail, and finally Wood, which swallows the coals — until Coyote teaches the Indians how to draw fire from wood by rubbing two dry sticks.
summary.zh: 世上唯一之火由三個 Skookums 看守於山頂，懼人類盜火而強盛。郊狼偽裝窺伺至黎明風起、守者入屋之隙，奪火下山。狼、松鼠（頸背烙黑、尾因而捲曲）、蛙（失其尾）接力傳火，火最終落入木中。郊狼教人以兩根乾木相鑽取火。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published fire-theft narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Cross-tradition fire-theft cluster (cf. Prometheus, Maui, Klamath/Nez Perce versions). Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Long ago men were hungry, cold and unhappy; the only fire in the world was on a mountain top, watched by three Skookums who guarded it carefully, for if men stole it they might become as strong as they. Coyote wanted men to be warm and happy. He crept to the mountain top and watched all day and all night, skulking in the bushes, while one Skookum sat always by the fire and another came out as she went in. Only when the dawn wind arose was there a chance: then the Skookum on guard, shivering, hurried into the tepee calling on her sister to watch the fire, and the sister was slow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 40 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote called a great council of the animals — he knew the Skookums would chase him — and skulked back to the peak. When the dawn wind rose and the Skookum went slowly in, Coyote seized the fire and jumped down the mountain. Skookum caught the tip of his tail, which is white to this day; then Wolf carried the fire; then Squirrel, leaping branch to branch, its neck scorched black and its tail curled by the heat; then Frog, which took the coals in its mouth and lost its tail to the Skookum's grip.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 40-41 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Skookum caught up again, Frog saved the fire by spitting it out on Wood, and Wood swallowed it. Skookum did not know how to get fire out of Wood — but Coyote did. He showed the Indians how to get fire from wood by rubbing two dry sticks together, as they do even to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 41 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: How Beaver Stole Fire from the Pine Trees

region.en: Grande Ronde River country, Nez Perce homeland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 格蘭德朗德河故地，內茲珀斯人家園（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected from Nez Perce narrators; retold 1910 (Judson)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'How Beaver Stole Fire' (Nez Perce)

summary.en: When only the Pine Trees hold the secret of fire and the animals almost freeze, Beaver hides under the river bank by the pines' great council fire, catches a rolling coal in his breast, and flees. The pines chase him down the winding Grande Ronde — whose crooked course is the mark of that pursuit — until Beaver swims the Snake River and gives fire to the willows, birches and other trees, from whose wood the Indians still make fire. Old Cedar, who ran to the hilltop to watch, stands there alone to this day.
summary.zh: 松樹獨掌火種，動物寒冬幾凍斃，遂議盜火。海狸先匿於松人大議之火旁河岸之下，拾一滾落火炭藏於胸，倉皇而逃。松林追之，格蘭德朗德河之曲直即追逃之痕。海狸渡斯內克河，以火授柳、樺諸木，印第安人至今鑽木取火。老雪松登丘瞭望，至今獨立丘頂。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Nez Perce narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Fire-theft cluster variant where the landscape (winding river, lone cedar) records the chase. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Long ago there were no people in the world; animals and trees talked and walked as men do now. The Pine Trees held the secret of fire and would tell no one: no one could have fire, however cold, unless he were a Pine. One winter it was so cold the animals almost froze, and they called a council to steal fire from the Pine Trees, who on the Grande Ronde River were holding a great council of their own around a large fire, with guards set to keep off all animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 42 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Beaver hid under the bank near the fire before the guards took their places. When a live coal rolled down the bank near him, he hid it in his breast and ran. The Pine Trees started after him, and Beaver dodged from side to side and ran straight ahead by turns — that is why the Grande Ronde winds in some places and is straight in others. The tired pines stopped on the river banks in crowds; a few pursued to the very end, standing here and there on the bank ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 42-43 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cedar ran to the top of a hill to watch how far ahead Beaver was, and saw him diving into Big Snake River where the Grande Ronde joins it. Beaver swam across, gave fire to the Willows on the far bank, then to the Birches and other trees — so these woods hold fire, and animals and Indians get it by rubbing two pieces together. Old Cedar still stands alone on the hilltop, his crown dead, with no other cedar within a hundred miles; the old men point him out to children, saying he stands just where he stopped when he chased Beaver.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 43 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bridge of the Gods

region.en: Cascade Locks on the Columbia River (Bridge of the Gods, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河喀斯喀特船閘（諸神之橋，象徵定位）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'The Bridge of the Gods'

summary.en: Tyhee Sahale comes down the Great River with his two sons, whose quarrel over the beautiful land he settles by shooting two arrows — north one to the first grandfather of the Klickitats, west one to the grandfather of the Multnomahs. He raises the Cascades between them and spans the river with the stone Bridge of the Tomanowos as a sign of peace. When fire is lost in a killing winter, Loo-wit's flame is shared on the bridge; her beauty kindles a feud between the chiefs Klickitat and Wiyeast, and Sahale, angry at the bloodshed, breaks the bridge, drowning the buried forests, and turns Loo-wit and her two suitors into the snow peaks St. Helens, Hood and Adams.
summary.zh: 大神 Tyhee Sahale 携二子下哥倫比亞河，二子爭奪美地；神射二箭定界，一在北為克利基特族祖，一在西為姆爾特諾馬族祖。神於兩族間聳立喀斯喀特山，復跨河建石橋（Tomanowos 之橋）為和平之證。大寒無火之時，以 Loo-wit 之火置橋上分授諸族；諸酋因戀其美色而戰，神怒，毀橋斷族，沉沒林中，並將三人化為白雪峰：聖海倫斯、胡德與亞當斯。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published mid-Columbia legend in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Sacred-landscape etiology of Cascade landmarks; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Long ago, when the world was new, Tyhee Sahale came down the Great River with his two sons, to where the Dalles now are. The land was very beautiful and each son wanted it; therefore they quarrelled. Sahale shot two arrows, one to the north and one to the west, and sent his sons to find them: where they lay, they should have the land. One son went over the plain to the country of the Klickitats, and was their first grandfather; the other followed the arrow to the Willamette Valley, and was the first grandfather of the Multnomahs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 47 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Sahale raised great mountains between the two countries, that the tribes might not quarrel — the Cascade Mountains — but made Great River deep and broad as a sign of peace, and built over it a great stone bridge, the Bridge of the Tomanowos. The tribes grew but did evil things and displeased Sahale; the sun ceased to shine, cold and snow came, and the people, fireless, tried to steal the fire of Loo-wit. Loo-wit fled, told Sahale of the Indians' need, and Sahale built a fire on the bridge of the gods where the people secured fire, promising Loo-wit eternal youth and beauty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 47-48 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the chiefs began to love Loo-wit. Two more chiefs came, Klickitat from the north and Wiyeast from the west; to neither would she give an answer, so the chiefs and their peoples fought. Because blood was shed and the river was no longer a sign of peace, Sahale broke down the bridge — great rocks fell into the river and buried forests can still be seen when the water is quiet — and turned Loo-wit, Klickitat and Wiyeast into snow peaks, cold and covered with ice forever: Mount St. Helens, Mount Hood and Mount Adams.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 48-49 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dalles: The Giants' Quarrel Blocks the River
title.zh: 達爾斯急灘：巨人相爭阻河

region.en: The Dalles of the Columbia River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河達爾斯急灘（象徵定位）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'The Dalles'

summary.en: After Sahale broke the Bridge of the Gods, Klickitat and Wiyeast still quarrelled over Loo-wit, and sheets of flame burst from their peaks as they threw great rocks at one another. Their throws fell short and the rocks dropped into the Great River, blocking it — which is why the river there is narrow and very swift, and why the place is called the Dalles.
summary.zh: 諸神之橋既毀，克利基特與 Wiyeast 二酋仍為 Loo-wit 相爭，山巔噴焰互擲巨石，擲不及遠，石落大河，河道為之壅塞——故其處河身窄而水急，是為達爾斯。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published mid-Columbia legend in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Continuation of the Bridge of the Gods narrative; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Long ago, after Sahale had broken down the bridge of the gods, Klickitat and Wiyeast still quarrelled over Loo-wit. When they quarrelled, sheets of flame burst from their peaks, and they threw great rocks at one another. But Klickitat and Wiyeast did not throw far enough: the rocks fell into the Great River and blocked it. Therefore the river is very narrow and very swift at that point — and thus it is called the Dalles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 50 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Story of Ashish: The Gambler Left in the Eagle's Nest
title.zh: 阿什什的故事：賭徒困於鷹巢

region.en: Klamath Lake country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯湖故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'The Story of Ashish' (Klamath)

summary.en: Ashish, the great gambler and archer with five wives, never misses the mark; Kemush, whose fire is only smoke and whose shots stray, plots against him. Feigning fear of an eagle-killing place, Kemush lures Ashish up a pine that grows to the sky beneath him, strands him starving in the nest, then dresses in his likeness and takes his place among the gamblers. The wives detect the fraud by Ashish's purple-blue fire and true aim; two butterflies find the wasted hero near the sky, feed him, and carry him home in a wildcat-lined basket.
summary.zh: 阿什什五妻、善賭善射，箭無虛發；其火呈紫藍。克穆什火僅冒煙、射輒偏，心生嫉恨。他假稱懼鷹巢殺地，誘阿什什攀松取鷹，松隨攀而長至天際，阿什什被困巢中，僅見雛鷺。克穆什易服冒充其歸，賭友與眾妻由火色與箭術識破。雙蝶近天發現骨瘦之阿什什，以筐攜食水往，鋪野貓皮載之還家。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klamath narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Deceiver-vs-hero tale with a sky-stranding motif. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Ashish, having many people with him, gambled on the way and shot at the target: Ashish hit it straight, Silver-Fox missed slightly, and Kemush hit only this side of the mark. About noon all the other men had lost all they had and gone to their lodges. Ashish had five wives — Mud Hen, Long-tail Squirrel, Sandhill Crane, Mallard and Chaffinch. Kemush plotted secretly against him, weeping and pretending to remember the place where his father had killed eagles, saying, 'Far away is the killing place of the young eagles; I kill them not, being afraid' — for Kemush coveted Little Squirrel, Ashish's wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 51-52 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Together they saw the eagles, and Kemush pointed out the pine for Ashish to climb. As Ashish climbed, the tree grew, until far up it touched the sky. At the top, Ashish found only the young of a lark in what was the eagle's eyrie, and wept. Kemush went away, dressed himself to appear like Ashish, and came back to the lodge; but the wives grew suspicious, and next morning, when the gambling party built its fire, only smoke curled up from Kemush's fire, and his shots strayed far from the mark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 52-53 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Four of Ashish's wives put pitch on their heads and wept, digging roots; only Mallard mourned not. Far away, close to the sky, Ashish was nothing but bones; two butterflies flew up near the sky, saw him, and told their father that a good man would soon perish. Next morning they flew up with a strung basket carrying food and water, raised Ashish, spread a wildcat's skin in the basket, and carried him down to the ground. He lay sick a long time, then recovered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 53-54 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Chinook Wind: Young Chinook's Revenge
title.zh: 欽諾克風：小欽諾克復仇

region.en: Yakima Valley and mid-Columbia (symbolic pin at Yakima)
region.zh: 亞基馬谷與中哥倫比亞（象徵定位於亞基馬）

texts.period: Collected from Yakima country narrators; retold 1910 (Judson)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Chinook Wind' (Takima)

summary.en: Five Chinook brothers on the Great River brought the warm wind; five Walla Walla brothers at the meeting of the waters brought the cold. In their first wrestling match, Coyote as judge let the last-spread ice defeat the last-spread oil, and beheaded the Chinooks. The eldest's orphan son grew mighty — uprooting firs like weeds — rescued his starving grandparents by outracing the fish-thieves with a speeding boat, and bathed them so that the washed-off straw and bark became the trout of Great River. In the second match Coyote let the oil be thrown last; four Walla Walla brothers fell and died, the fifth yielded, and the winds were tamed forever.
summary.zh: 哥倫比亞河畔欽諾克五兄弟掌暖風，瓦拉瓦拉五兄弟掌寒風，兩黨相爭不休。初賽摔角，郊狼為判官，暗令兩家祖父母撒油與冰，冰後撒者勝，欽諾克五兄弟盡斬。長兄遺孤小欽諾克力能拔杉如草，以疾舟衝破搶魚者，護祖捕魚；浴祖時，沖下草屑鱗介化為河中鱒魚。再賽，郊狼令油後撒，瓦拉瓦拉四兄弟倒斃，其五投降解散寒風，暖冬乃定。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Yakima-country narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Wind-war etiology; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once five brothers lived on Great River — the Chinook brothers, who caused the warm wind to blow — and five other brothers at Walla Walla, the meeting of the waters, who caused the cold wind. Their grandparents all lived at Umatilla, the place of wind-drifted sands. The two sets of brothers were always fighting, sweeping the country with wind, blowing down trees, raising dust, freezing the rivers and thawing them into floods, so that it was very hard for the people. At last the Walla Walla brothers challenged the Chinooks to wrestle: whoever fell should have his head cut off. Coyote was made judge, and also headsman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 70 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote secretly told the Chinooks' grandparents to throw oil on the ground so their sons would not fall, and the Walla Walla grandparents to throw ice. Both threw, but the Walla Walla side threw last; the ground was slippery, and the Chinook brothers fell one after another, and Coyote cut off their heads. But the oldest Chinook brother had a baby son, whose mother taught him he must revenge his father and uncles. Young Chinook grew so strong he could pull up large fir trees and throw them around like weeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 70-71 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: He found his grandparents at Umatilla cold and hungry, for the Walla Walla brothers blew the northeast wind always and stole their fish. Young Chinook lay hidden in the boat while his grandfather fished, and the boat shot ahead whenever the thieves came near, so the fish were landed safe. Then he bathed his grandparents, and all the straw and grass and bark washed off them became trout in Great River. In the second wrestling match Coyote had the oil thrown last: four Walla Walla brothers fell and were beheaded, the fifth yielded and was warned to blow lightly and never freeze the people again, while Young Chinook was told to blow hardest only at night and first on the mountain ridges to warn the people. Thus now winter is only a little cold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 71-73 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Cry-because-he-had-no-wife

region.en: Nez Perce homeland, Idaho (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯人故地，愛達荷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected from Nez Perce narrators; retold 1910 (Judson)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Cry-because-he-had-no-wife' (Nez Perce)

summary.en: A crying orphan boy weeps day and night because he wants a wife, and is sent east to a maiden guarded by a man-killing horse. Passing a giant's house he politely takes the one small (venison) roast among four human legs; he slips past Cliff-Giant as a little dog; he blinds the guard-horse's attention with two spat-upon stones. The maiden names him, baths him to man's size, and the two flee her home on the horse, dropping whips of black haw, smoke-wood, mud, slide-rock, red haw and big mountains to tangle, mire, wound and finally wall off the pursuing giant.
summary.zh: 孤兒日夜啼哭，因欲得妻，遂被遣往東方娶守於殺人駿馬之女。途經巨人宅，辨識四條人腿烤肉，僅取小鹿肉；化身小狗疾行避過巖崖巨人；以吐口涎之石二度絆開護衛駿馬，得入女宅。少女呼其名，浴之成人身。二人騎馬逃歸，沿途擲黑楂、煙木、泥、滑石、紅楂、大山等六鞭，纏絆、陷溺、割裂巨人，終以山嶺阻其追擊。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Nez Perce narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Monster-avoidance quest tale; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once there was a little orphan boy who cried day and night; his grandmother asked why, and he said, 'I cry because I want a wife.' His grandparents knew of a girl who lived toward the east and sent him there. On the trail he came to a giant's house, who asked him to stay to breakfast: the giant had four large roasts and one small one on the fire. The boy picked out the small roast — the four large ones were the legs of people the giant had killed, the small one venison, as his grandmother had taught him. 'Never eat too much.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 81 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he came to a great rock cliff, Cliff-Giant, which crushed people; he turned himself into a little dog and, watching for the cliff to move, ran under it fast and escaped. The girl's lodge was guarded by a great horse that killed people before they could reach it. The boy, still crying, spat all over a large stone and threw it behind him; the horse stopped to stamp on it, and he threw the second stone just before he reached the lodge and jumped in. The girl knew him at once and called him by name — Iwapnep Atswitki, Cry-because-he-had-no-wife. After a bath he became of man's size.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 81-82 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning they rode toward his home, making whips that could speak as they went: a black-haw whip that could outlast all others, a smoke-wood whip to tangle the giant, a mud whip to mire him, a slide-rock whip to trouble his passage, a red-haw whip to tear his flesh, and a whip of big mountains he could not get past. When the giant rushed out crying 'Give me your wife!', the boy sent him for water and whipped away; whip after whip was thrown down until the whip of high mountains fell and the giant could not cross it. Thus they escaped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 83-84 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Naming of Creation

region.en: Nez Perce homeland, Idaho (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯人故地，愛達荷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected from Nez Perce narrators; retold 1910 (Judson)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'The Naming of Creation' (Nez Perce)

summary.en: Coyote, chief of all the animals, announces that the tribes of men are coming, and that tomorrow they will come out of the ground to be named by him and spread out. He names every people as they emerge — but when the people are all out, he finds he has kept no name for himself, and so names himself Coyote. Thus came all people, not the Nez Perce alone.
summary.zh: 郊狼為百獸之首，預言明日人類諸族將出地面，由他命名而散居四方。翌日人群湧出，郊狼逐一命名；然族人盡出，卻未為自己留名，遂自名為『郊狼』。眾人由是而生——非獨內茲珀斯人，乃普世之人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Nez Perce narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Ethnogony (origin of the peoples) centered on naming; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was chief of all the animals. He told them that the tribes of men were coming near, one and all, and everything he told them came true. Then he said, 'Tomorrow the people will come out of the ground. I will name them and they will spread out.' Then he named them; he named them until he had named them all. And the people came out, but Coyote had no name for himself. Many people came out. Then he named himself Coyote. Thus came people — not we alone, but all people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 86 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bird Chief

region.en: Nez Perce country, Idaho-Oregon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯人故地，愛達荷—俄勒岡（象徵定位）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'The Bird Chief'

summary.en: The birds gather and declare that whichever, flying farthest, can reach the upper world shall be chief. Every bird rises to equal heights and returns wing-tired; Eagle alone climbs higher, and all think him certain of the crown. But Wren has hidden beneath Eagle's thick wing feathers on the ascent, and when Eagle can go no higher, Wren flies beyond him. Eagle returns proud and alone; Wren, after a long wait, comes back — and is made chief.
summary.zh: 眾鳥集議：飛得最高、能達上天者為王。群鳥力竭皆返，唯鷹獨上更高，自以為勝券在握；而鷦鷯藏於鷹翼厚羽間同行，待鷹力竭，鷦鷯再飛越其上。鷹傲然而歸，眾候鷦鷯久久始返——竟立鷦鷯為百鳥之王。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Plateau narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Humility-contest etiology; category 'myth'.

passages.text: They called all the birds and said: 'The bird which, flying farthest, can reach the upper world, shall be chief.' All the birds high in the air went to equal heights; Wren sat beneath the thick feathers of Eagle's wing as Eagle flew. Wing-tired, the birds returned to earth; only Eagle went above, and when he had gone as high as he could, Wren flew beyond him. The birds waited below; Eagle returned alone after a long time, too highly thinking of himself — and behold, Wren, returning at length, was made chief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 87 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Spell of the Laughing Raven

region.en: Klamath Lake country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯湖故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'The Spell of the Laughing Raven' (Klamath)

summary.en: At the dance place of the Klamath Lake people, Old Raven laughs at the dancers, and everyone dancing there becomes rock. Later, Old Gray Wolf lies asleep in full regalia; Old Grizzly steals his beaded moccasins, is caught and rolled down the rocks to his death — and when the Klamath people fight the Northerners over the killing, Old Raven laughs again, and the fighters become rocks.
summary.zh: 克拉斯湖人在舞場起舞，老鴉一笑，舞者盡化石。其後老灰狼盛裝臥眠，老灰熊竊其珠履，被覺而遭滾石擊斃；克拉斯人與北方人因之開戰，老鴉再笑，參戰者亦盡化石。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klamath narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim.石化 motif tied to landscape; category 'myth'.

passages.text: At 'dance place' when the Klamath Lake people danced, many people were there, and Kemush, Old Man of the Ancients, went there too. Then Old Raven laughed at them as they danced, and all the people dancing there became rocks. Gray Wolf entered Kitti from the north, and stopped and lay down in full dress — moccasins with beads on the toe — though he had not yet reached his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 88 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old Grizzly approached the sleeping Gray Wolf and stole his moccasins and beads, putting them on to go to the fishing place. Gray Wolf woke, threw Old Grizzly down the hill, and rolled him over the rocks until he died, for having robbed him. Then the Klamath Lake people began fighting the Northerners because Old Grizzly had been killed — and Old Raven laughed at them as they fought, and they became rocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 88 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Memaloose Islands

region.en: Memaloose Islands near The Dalles, Columbia River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河達爾斯附近亡靈島（象徵定位）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'The Memaloose Islands' (Klickitat)

summary.en: A young chief dies with no rest in the land of the spirits, and a vision sends his grieving maiden up Great River to the spirit island, where four spirit people meet her and she dances all night with her lover. At sunrise the dancers are skeletons, and she flees home across the river in an old boat; her frightened father returns her to the island. In time a half-human, half-spirit child is born, and its grandmother, warned not to look on it until ten days old, lifts the cloth one little corner — so the baby dies, and the spirits forbid the living ever again to visit the land of the dead.
summary.zh: 青年酋長亡後在冥土不安，其未婚妻夢受指引，隨父泛舟上溯大河至靈島，夜與亡夫共舞。天明舞者盡成白骨，女驚駭駕殘舟逃歸；父懼其禍及族人，復送之回島。其後誕下半人半靈之嬰，祖母急欲一見，未及十日即掀巾一角，嬰遂夭，靈界遂禁生人再訪亡者之國。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klickitat narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Journey to the land of the dead with a broken viewing taboo; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Long ago, before the white man came, a young chief and a maiden loved one another. Suddenly the chief went over the spirit trail, but could find no rest in the land of the spirits, and the maiden also grieved for him. A vision told her to go to the land of the spirits; her father obeyed, made ready a canoe, and they paddled up Great River to the spirit island. Through the darkness they heard singing and the tom-tom of the dance drum, and four spirit people met them on the shore. The maiden landed; her father returned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 98 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the great dance house the maiden met her lover, more beautiful than on earth, and all night they danced. When morning came and the robins chirped, the dancers fell asleep; the maiden woke to find skeletons and skulls all around her, her lover gazing with grinning teeth. Struck with horror she ran to the shore, found an old boat, and paddled herself across Great River to the Indian village — but her father was frightened, for one who had been to the spirit land would bring evil on the tribe, and that night he paddled her back to the memaloose island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 98-99 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: In course of time a baby, half human, half spirit, was born. The spirit lover sent a messenger telling his mother to come by night, and warned her not to look at the baby until it was ten days old. She became impatient, lifted one little corner of the cloth from the baby's face, and the baby died. The spirit people were displeased, and said that never again should living people visit the land of those who had gone by the spirit trail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 99 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Origin of the Tribes: Coyote and Wishpoosh the Monster Beaver
title.zh: 諸族之始：郊狼與巨狸維什普什

region.en: Lake Cle-el-lum and Kittitas Valley, Yakima country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 克利埃勒姆湖與基蒂塔斯谷，亞基馬故地（象徵定位）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Origin of the Tribes' (Chinook/Wishpoosh cycle)

summary.en: Wishpoosh, the monster beaver of Lake Cle-el-lum, drowns and devours the animal people who come to fish. Coyote, spear lashed to his wrist, is dragged through a chain of bursting lakes — Cle-el-lum, Kittitas, Toppenish, the great lake at the rivers' meeting — the tearing of each bank carving the river's course, down to the breakers of the Bitter Waters. He drifts back as a branch, is swallowed, cuts the sinews inside Wishpoosh with his stone knife, and dismembers the carcass: head into the Nez Perce, arms into the Cayuses, legs into the Klickitats, ribs into the Yakimas, belly into the Chinooks, hair and blood flung east to become the Snake River Indians.
summary.zh: 克利埃勒姆湖巨狸維什普什溺殺並吞噬前來捕魚之獸人。郊狼縛矛於腕往捕，被拖穿一連串決堤之湖——克利埃勒姆、基蒂塔斯、托皮尼什、三江匯流之巨湖——堤岸屢破，河道由此成形，直至苦水之海口。郊狼化樹枝漂回，被吞，以石刀割斷其體內之筋而殺之，並分其屍：首化內茲珀斯人，臂化卡尤斯人，腿化克利基特人，肋化亞基馬人，腹化欽諾克人，髮血擲東成蛇河諸部。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published mid-Columbia narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Ethnogony via dismemberment, a strong cross-tradition parallel (Ymir, Pangu, Purusha, Popol Vuh). Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Long ago, in Lake Cle-el-lum, lived Wishpoosh, the monster beaver. The lake was beautiful and full of fish, and the animal people wanted to fish there; but Wishpoosh killed them, dragging them into the water and drowning them, and ate them. At last Coyote tried to kill him: he fastened a spear to his wrist with a strong cord and began to fish. Wishpoosh attacked, Coyote speared him, and the beaver plunged to the bottom, dragging Coyote with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 102 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: They fought so hard they tore out the banks of Cle-el-lum, and the waters rushed through the mountains and down the canon into Kittitas Valley, forming a lake there; they tore out those banks too, and the waters flooded Yakima and formed a great lake at Toppenish; those banks also broke, and the waters formed a very great lake where the Yakima, the Snake and the Columbia meet. Wishpoosh dashed down the Great River, Coyote catching at trees and stones along the banks in vain, until they reached the breakers of the Bitter Waters at the mouth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 102-103 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wishpoosh killed and swallowed salmon and whales. Coyote, remembering he was the wisest and cunningest of all the animals, changed himself into a tree branch, drifted toward Wishpoosh, and was swallowed. Inside, he changed back, took his stone knife, and cut the sinews inside Wishpoosh, so that Wishpoosh died. With Muskrat's help he pulled the great beaver to land and cut him up, throwing the pieces over the country: from the head the Nez Perces, great in council; from the arms the Cayuses, powerful with bow and war-club; from the legs the Klickitats, famous runners; from the ribs the Yakimas; from the belly the Chinooks. The hair and blood he flung far east, and they became the Snake River Indians, a tribe of war and blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 103-104 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Okanogans Became Red

region.en: Okanogan country, Washington-British Columbia (symbolic pin at Okanogan)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地，華盛頓—不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'How the Okanogans Became Red' (Okanogan)

summary.en: On far-off Samahtumiwhoolah, White Man's Island, the white giants war among themselves until their queen Scomalt breaks off their piece of land and pushes it out to sea. Storms kill all but one man and one woman, who live on whale blubber until the island sinks; they paddle for many suns to the young mainland, where the sun has burned them red. All the Okanogans descend from this pair — and the tale ends with the world's end: in time the lakes will melt the world's foundations, and it will float away like the island did.
summary.zh: 極海之島 Samahtumiwhoolah（白人之島）上，白巨人內戰不休，女王 Scomalt 怒而斷其陸、足踢出海。風暴吞沒島民，唯餘一男一女，賴鯨脂維生；島沉，二人划舟多日抵尚在成長之大陸，日炙其膚而赤。奧卡諾根人皆其後裔。末預言世界末日：湖水終將蝕世基，大地將如孤島漂流，是為 Itsowleigh。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Okanogan narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Ethnogony and end-of-world prophecy; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Long ago, when the sun was young and no bigger than a star, there was an island far out at sea called Samahtumiwhoolah, White Man's Island. Giants lived there; they were white, and their leader was a tall white woman, Scomalt. At first there was peace, but at last war came and the white giants fought with each other. Scomalt, whose heart was strong, drove the unruly ones to the farthest end of the island, broke off that piece of land, and pushed it out to sea with her foot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 105 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Many days the floating island drifted; storms swept over it and the sun beat down, until all had died except one man and one woman. They caught a whale and saved their lives on the blubber; then, as the island began to sink, they made a canoe, put the blubber in, and paddled away. After many suns they came to islands and at last to the mainland, which was not so large as now, for it had not yet grown. All their whiteness was gone: the sun had burned them until they were red. All the Okanogans are descended from this man and woman, and therefore they are red.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 105-106 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: In time to come, the lakes will melt the foundations of the world and the rivers will cut it loose; then the whole world will float as the island did. This is the end of the world, the Itsowleigh.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 106 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Origin of Mineral Springs: The Twins and the Bitter Waters
title.zh: 礦泉起源：雙生子與苦水

region.en: Klamath country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Origin of Mineral Springs'

summary.en: In the peaceful days of the first grandfather, when the firs were no larger than arrows, the first twins are born: one a famous hunter, the other always hungry. Hunting together, the hungry brother leans over a spring to drink, and his twin strikes him with a stone tomahawk and pushes him in; the water boils, and from the vapor rises the first of all Indians, who curses the murderer: wherever he drinks, the waters shall be bitter. So the springs are bitter — and for that reason, the teller adds, twins were not allowed to live.
summary.zh: 初祖太平之世，巨杉猶細如箭，誕下首對雙生子：一名獵聲赫赫，一名恆飢。同獵之時，飢者俯泉欲飲，其弟以石斧擊其首推之入泉；泉水沸騰，蒸霧中現首印第安人，詛兇手：『凡爾所飲之處，其水必苦。』故今之泉多苦——言者又云，因此俗禁雙生子併存。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Judson gives no tribe; placed in the Klamath/camas-root Plateau belt as a conservative reading. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Long ago, in the days of the first grandfather, all men were at peace, and the earth was so new that the tall firs of the mountain were no larger than arrows. Many fish swam in Beautiful Waters and Great River, many deer on the mountains, many ipo and camas roots in the valley. Then the first twins were born: one became famous for the deer he shot and the fish he speared; the other was always hungry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 108 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the brothers were hunting together. One leaned over the spring to drink; his brother struck him on the head with his stone tomahawk and pushed him into the spring. At once the water bubbled and boiled, and from a cloud of vapor arose an old Indian, the first of all, who said, 'You have sharpened the tomahawk against your brother. Go. Wander. Wherever you drink, the waters shall be bitter.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 108 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The brother wandered over the mountains and plains, and wherever he drank the waters became bitter. For that reason, the story says, the Indians did not allow twins to live: one is always unlucky and the other happy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 108 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and Grizzly: The Sick Bear and the Broken Bridge
title.zh: 郊狼與灰熊：病熊與斷橋

region.en: Nez Perce homeland, Idaho (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯人故地，愛達荷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected from Nez Perce narrators; retold 1910 (Judson)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Coyote and Grizzly' (Nez Perce)

summary.en: An always-angry grizzly devours a whole band of Indians and nearly dies of her meal; she sends for Coyote as medicine man. He cures her, lets the people flee, and then tells the truth — she has eaten too many Indians. The chase begins: Coyote becomes a buffalo grazing by the trail, then a smallpox-stricken old man in a tepee, and points the pursuing bear to a willow bridge; she steps on it, it breaks, and she is drowned, to the delight of the people.
summary.zh: 常怒之灰熊吞食整隊印第安人，幾乎脹死，請郊狼為醫。郊狼施術癒之，俟眾人逃散後始言真相：『妳食人多矣。』灰熊暴起追之。郊狼先化路旁食草之水牛，繼化帳中患痘老人，指熊過柳條橋；橋斷熊落水溺斃。郊狼復原形歸告族人：已誅灰熊。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Nez Perce narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Trickster-beats-cannibal tale; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once there was a grizzly bear who was always angry. Travelling through the woods she came upon a band of Indians and ate them all. That evening her head ached, and in the night she grew very sick, for she had eaten so many Indians; she was sick a week and nearly died, and sent for Coyote to come as a medicine man. Coyote told his friends he did not care if she died — everybody would be glad — but at his wife's urging he went, made medicine, and she recovered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 114 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: He told her she was sick from eating too many chokecherries, thinking all the people would run away if he told the truth; but when the people were gone and he himself ready to run, he said she had eaten too many Indians. Old Grizzly jumped up and chased him. He ran up the hills, down the valleys, through the woods, and at last changed himself into a buffalo eating grass by the trail. Grizzly started to kill the buffalo, but seeing Coyote's trail run past it, she followed the trail — and Coyote, back in his own shape, called after her: 'You are only a foolish old bear. You can never catch me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 115 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: She started after him again. Then Coyote changed himself into an old man who had smallpox, in a tepee by the trail, his clothes old and worn. When Grizzly came up and asked if anyone had passed, he said a man had crossed the river, and showed her a willow bridge with tracks on it. She walked on it; the bridge broke, she fell into the water and was drowned. Coyote turned himself back and told his people he had killed Grizzly Bear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 115 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Origin of Spokane Falls

region.en: Spokane Falls, Spokane River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斯波坎河斯波坎瀑布（象徵定位）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Origin of Spokane Falls' (Flathead)

summary.en: Travelling up the river with Fox, Coyote declares he will marry a woman of the Pend d'Oreilles and asks their chief for a wife. The chief refuses: Pend d'Oreille women may not intermarry with other tribes. Coyote answers that he will make a falls here in the river so the salmon cannot get past — and that is how Spokane Falls were made.
summary.zh: 郊狼與狐狸溯河而行，至斯波坎瀑布處，欲娶彭德奧雷伊人之女，求於其酋長。酋長拒之，謂其族女不得與他族通婚。郊狼遂言：『吾將於此河造瀑，使鮭不得上溯。』斯波坎瀑布由是而成。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Flathead narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Place-etiology with marriage-rule theme; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox were travelling together up the river. When they got to where Spokane Falls now are, Coyote said to Fox: 'I believe I'll get married. I'll take a woman of the Pend d'Oreilles for my wife.' So Coyote went to visit the chief of the Pend d'Oreilles and said he wanted a wife. The chief said no — Pend d'Oreille women could not intermarry with other tribes. Coyote said, 'Then I will make a falls here in the river. I will make falls so that the salmon cannot get past them.' That is how Spokane Falls were made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 118 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Salmon: Breaking the Skookums' Dam

region.en: Klamath River country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 克拉馬斯河故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected from Klamath River narrators; retold 1910 (Judson)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Coyote and the Salmon' (Klamath River)

summary.en: The Klamath River people starve while the river is full of salmon, for three Skookums have dammed the fish out. Coyote whines at their camp for fish until he sees where the dam's key is kept; next morning he trips the Skookum who carries it, opens the dam, and the salmon run upstream into the country of the Cahrocs so the people have food. Afterwards he breaks down the dam entirely — which is why salmon go up that river every year.
summary.zh: 克拉馬斯河鮭魚盈河而民飢，蓋三 Skookums 築壩阻魚。郊狼詐乞於其營，窺得壩鑰所在；翌晨絆倒攜鑰之 Skookum，取鑰啟壩，鮭魚上溯至 Cahrocs 之地，民乃得食。事後並毀其壩，故鮭魚歲歲上溯此河。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klamath River narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Salmon-liberation culture-hero episode (cf. Okanagon/Nez Perce versions); category 'myth'.

passages.text: Then Coyote went to Klamath River. He found the people very poor; they had no food, though the river was full of salmon. Three Skookums had built a dam to keep the salmon from coming up the river; the Skookums had all the fish, the people none. Coyote was very angry and said: 'Before many suns, fish shall come up the river. The people shall have all the salmon they need.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 123 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went to the mouth of the river and whined for fish; the Skookums drove him away, thinking him only a skulking coyote — but he had seen where they kept the key of the dam, which was what he wanted. Next morning, when a Skookum started down to open the trap and let in a fish for herself, Coyote ran out of the tepee, jumped between her feet and tripped her up; the key fell from her hand, he picked it up and went to the dam, opened it, and the salmon went upstream into the country of the Cahrocs. The people had food. Afterwards Coyote broke down the dam, and ever since salmon go up that river every year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 123-124 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: How Coyote Was Killed by the Star

region.en: Sky-world descent to a mountain top (symbolic pin, southern Oregon highlands)
region.zh: 自天界降於山巔（象徵定位，俄勒岡南部高地）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'How Coyote Was Killed'

summary.en: Having stolen fire from the Skookums and given salmon to the Indians, Coyote, thinking highly of himself, demands that the Star which comes each night close to his mountain carry him to the sky world. The Star only laughs, until at last it agrees. Coyote leaps and clings to its edge; the sky grows colder and colder, his paws slip, and he falls for ten snows, striking the earth crushed flat as a willow mat. Thus Coyote was killed.
summary.zh: 郊狼既盜火、又授鮭，自視甚高，欲遊天界。每夜近山之星受其嘮叨而不答，終允載之。郊狼躍攀星緣，天寒徹骨，爪滑墜落，歷十場雪始觸地，壓扁如葦席。郊狼由是而死。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Trickster's death by hubris — the fall-from-sky episode closing the fire/salmon cycle. Pin is symbolic. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote had done many things: fire he had stolen from the Skookums, and salmon he had given to the Indians. Therefore, thinking very highly of himself, he wanted to travel to the sky world. Now Star came every night very close to Coyote, who lived above the clouds on a mountain top. Coyote said to Star, 'Take me with you,' but Star only laughed; still Coyote asked every night, and still Star laughed, until Coyote howled at him. At last Star said, 'Tomorrow night I will take you to the sky world.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 131 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next night Star came again, quite close, and Coyote leaped far and caught on the edge of Star, and they travelled through the sky world. Star climbed higher and higher; Coyote looked down and the tall firs of the forest were only as large as arrows. Coyote grew cold, for Star was not warm like Sun, until he could not hold on: his paws slipped and he fell. For ten snows he fell, and when he struck the earth he was crushed as flat as a willow mat. Thus Coyote was killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 131-132 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Old Grizzly and Old Antelope

region.en: Klamath Lake country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯湖故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

texts.period: Collected from Klamath Lake narrators; retold 1910 (Judson)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Old Grizzly and Old Antelope' (Klamath Lake)

summary.en: Two mothers, Old Grizzly and Old Antelope, dig ipo roots together; the lazy bear, pretending to pick insects from her companion's fur, crunches ipo roots in her teeth and bites Old Antelope through the neck, serving the flesh to both sets of children. The young antelopes recognize the taste of their mother and, while Old Grizzly is out, kill her cubs in a game of 'smoke in, smoke out' in the lodge, gag and paint the corpses so Old Grizzly is deceived, then escape — surviving a false voice-trap, a flight to Old Crane, and finally, crossing the water, killing Old Grizzly herself with arrows borrowed from the Crane children.
summary.zh: 老灰熊與老羚羊同掘伊波根；灰熊假稱為伴啄蟲，實以伊波根塞齒作咬物之聲，咬斷羚羊之頸而殺之，並以其肉分飼兩家孩子。小羚羊嘗出母肉之味，趁灰熊外出，與其子女玩『煙入煙出』之戲而悶斃熊崽，並以紅彩、鼻鉗佈置死狀騙過灰熊。二孩逃往老鶴家，藏於哨笛；灰熊追至，渡河時因擊鶴腿傾覆，老鶴怒射之，小羚羊亦借弓箭射殺灰熊。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klamath Lake narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Contains animal-children revenge theme; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Old Grizzly lived with Old Antelope; each had two children. Going out to dig ipo roots, Old Antelope always filled her basket while Old Grizzly dug little and ate what she dug. Pretending that insects bit her, Old Grizzly begged Old Antelope to bite into her fur, then wished to bite into Old Antelope's fur in return. She put ipo roots into her mouth and, crunching them as if cracking insects, bit Old Antelope through the neck and killed her, then cut her up wholly, hiding the meat under the ipo roots on top of a pole, and gave meat to her own children and to Old Antelope's children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 133-134 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The younger antelope child said, 'It tastes like our mother'; the elder pushed her: 'Be silent.' Next morning, Old Grizzly gone to fetch the meat, the young antelopes suggested games their mother had forbidden: skipping down from the lodge, jumping logs, diving, and at last 'smoke out'. They threw rotten wood into the lodge; the cubs went in, covered the smoke hole, and the antelopes chanted 'Two smoke in, two smoke out... smother, smother,' until the cubs were dead. The antelopes painted the corpses' faces with red paint, gagged them, lifted one to the top of the lodge and fastened one on the ladder, then hid in the fireplace, enjoining every article of the lodge not to tell Old Grizzly — all except the bone awl stuck in the roof.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 135-137 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old Grizzly returned, called for the children, and the articles answered her from every side until the forgotten awl Shakta spoke: 'Long ago the children went away; through here they crawled, and placed coals against the opening.' She broke through and pursued them, weeping that rotten wood breaks easily. She overtook them camping in a cave, but they threw sticks at her until sure she slept, then fled to Old Crane, who blew them into a whistle stick and hung them in his lodge. When Grizzly demanded to be set across, Old Crane let her walk on his outstretched leg; in mid-river she struck his leg with the drinking cup to shake the water out, and the angered Crane doused her in the river, shot her with a bow, and the young antelopes came out of the whistle and, with bows borrowed from the Crane children, shot her until she was dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 137-140 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Legend of the Klickitat Basket

region.en: Klickitat country, mid-Columbia River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 克利基特故地，中哥倫比亞河（象徵定位）

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Legend of the Klickitat Basket' (Klickitat)

summary.en: Shade commands the first Weaver to weave tooksi, the basket. Her first basket, woven of yi and squaw, elk and pine grass with red cedar roots, leaks; Weaver mourns by the lake until the clear water itself shows her the pattern, chato-timus. Weaving again with red cedar roots she makes a tight basket with the pattern in it, and other weavers learn it — which is why Klickitat baskets are plenty, do not leak, and carry a pattern.
summary.zh: 影神命首位織者編籃（tooksi）。初織以茅草、松草、紅杉根等，成而漏水；織者臨湖悲泣，忽見清水中現紋樣 chato-timus，遂再入林取紅杉根重織。新籃不漏且有紋。他織者從而學之——故克利基特人籃多、不漏且皆有紋。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klickitat narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Craft-origin legend; category 'myth'.

passages.text: Shade told the first weaver to weave tooksi, the basket. Weaver said, 'I do not know how.' But she went to the forest and thought a long time how to weave tooksi; then she gathered the plant yi, with squaw grass, elk grass, pine grass, and noo-wi-ash, the red cedar roots. Working very hard for many days, she finished the basket and carried it to the lake; she dipped it full of water, but the water leaked out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, p. 141 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Shade said, 'It will not do. Weave again. Weave a tight basket with a pattern in it.' Weaver sat by the lake mourning, until at last, in the clear water, she saw the pattern, chato-timus, and was happy again. She went back into the deep forest, pulled up the red cedar roots, and worked many days. This time, dipped full, the basket did not leak, and it had the pattern on it as Shade had told her. Other weavers learned the pattern; thus the Klickitats have plenty of baskets that do not leak and have a pattern in them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 141-142 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.
